lead: This unit is about the integral: adding infinitely many small pieces to get a total, and using that total to measure area, length, volume and surface. After it you can evaluate definite and improper integrals, use the gamma and beta functions, and set up area, arc length and revolution problems. You also learn the fundamental theorem that connects integration with differentiation.
about: The unit builds the integral as a sum of small pieces, then uses it to measure shape. Chapter 2.1 defines the definite integral, Riemann sums and the fundamental theorem; Chapter 2.2 supplies indefinite integrals and the standard techniques. Chapter 2.3 treats improper integrals by limits, and Chapter 2.4 uses them to define the gamma and beta functions. Chapter 2.5 applies definite integrals to area between curves; Chapter 2.6 applies the same idea to arc length; Chapter 2.7 extends it to volume and surface area of revolution. The chapters move from the definition and computation of an integral to geometric measurement. Some topics are advanced and marked in their chapters.

chapters.idea: A definite integral is a limit of sums, and the fundamental theorem turns it into a difference of antiderivative values.
chapters.depth: Cover Riemann sums, the definite integral ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx as a limit, basic properties (linearity, additivity over intervals), and the two parts of the fundamental theorem: d/dx ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt = f(x), and ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a) when F′ = f. Include the net change theorem as the applied form. Some syllabi call this the fundamental theorem of calculus. Define f, a, b, x, t and F. Keep proofs short and intuitive; use Unit 1 derivatives.

figure.aria: The curve f(x)=3x²+2x and its antiderivative F(x)=x³+x² from x=0 to 2; the area under f from 0 to 2 equals F(2)−F(0)=12.

chapters.example: Evaluate ∫₀² (3x² + 2x) dx by the fundamental theorem; show the value is 12.
chapters.trap: Forgetting the lower limit: F(b) − F(a), not F(b), and not F(a) − F(b).
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: limits, continuity and derivatives; Chapter 2.1 uses derivative rules.
chapters.leave: Leave rigorous epsilon proofs of integrability and properties of the Riemann integral to an analysis course; leave double integrals to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: An indefinite integral is an antiderivative family, and each integration technique reverses a differentiation rule.
chapters.depth: Cover standard antiderivatives, the constant C, substitution (reverse chain rule), integration by parts (reverse product rule), partial fractions, and simple trigonometric integrals. Include choosing u and dv, and checking by differentiation. Some syllabi call substitution the change of variable. Do not prove every standard form; practise the common ones. Connect to Chapter 2.1 for evaluation of definite integrals by substitution.

figure.aria: The flow starts with ∫ x e²ˣ dx, splits into u=x with dv=e²ˣ dx and du=dx with v=½e²ˣ, then the parts formula, ending at ½x e²ˣ − ¼e²ˣ + C.

chapters.example: Evaluate ∫ x e²ˣ dx by integration by parts; show the result is (x/2)e²ˣ − (1/4)e²ˣ + C.
chapters.trap: Dropping +C in an indefinite integral, or choosing u and dv so the new integral is harder.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1 and Unit 1: derivative rules, product rule and chain rule.
chapters.leave: Leave Laplace transforms and differential equations to their own units; leave beta and gamma integrals to Chapter 2.4.

chapters.idea: An improper integral is a limit of proper integrals when the interval is infinite or the integrand blows up.
chapters.depth: Cover improper integrals of the first kind (infinite interval) and second kind (unbounded integrand), convergence and divergence by limits, p-integrals ∫₁^∞ x^(−p) dx and ∫₀¹ x^(−p) dx, and the comparison test. Define limit R→∞ and limit c→a⁺ or b⁻. Mention absolute convergence. Some syllabi call these improper integrals of first and second kind. Keep proofs of comparison short.

figure.aria: The curve y=1/x² from x=1 to 10; the area from 1 to R tends to 1 as R grows.

chapters.example: Show that ∫₁^∞ x^(−2) dx converges and find its value; show the limit is 1.
chapters.trap: Treating ∞ as a number and substituting it directly; write a limit and check both endpoints or both tails.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2.1 and 2.2: definite integrals, antiderivatives and limits.
chapters.leave: Leave series convergence tests and Cauchy sequences to Unit 3; leave numerical integration to a numerical methods unit.

chapters.idea: The gamma and beta functions are integrals that extend factorial and give a compact way to evaluate many definite integrals.
chapters.depth: Define Γ(x) = ∫₀^∞ t^(x−1) e^(−t) dt for x > 0, and B(p,q) = ∫₀¹ t^(p−1)(1−t)^(q−1) dt for p,q > 0. Cover Γ(n+1)=n!, Γ(1)=1, B(p,q)=Γ(p)Γ(q)/Γ(p+q), symmetry B(p,q)=B(q,p), and simple evaluations. Some syllabi call these Eulerian integrals. Mention convergence from Chapter 2.3; do not prove the duplication formula unless a syllabus lists it.

figure.aria: The block flow from Γ(5)=24 and B(2,3) to the beta formula, then to the substitution 1!·2!/4!, ending at 1/12.

chapters.example: Evaluate B(2,3) using the gamma function; check that the value is 1/12.
chapters.trap: Using Γ(p+q) in the denominator but p! q! in the numerator without shifting: Γ(n+1)=n!, so Γ(5)=4!, not 5!.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.3 for improper integrals and Chapter 2.2 for substitution; factorial notation.
chapters.leave: Leave double and triple integrals of beta and gamma type to Unit 5; leave Laplace transforms of special functions to their own unit.

chapters.idea: The area between two curves is the integral of the upper curve minus the lower curve over the interval between their intersection points.
chapters.depth: Advanced: only a few universities teach this. Cover vertical slices ∫ₐᵇ (top − bottom) dx and horizontal slices ∫_c^d (right − left) dy, finding intersection points, splitting the interval when the top and bottom swap, and using symmetry. Some syllabi call this area of a region between curves. Keep to single integrals; do not use double integrals.

figure.aria: The curves y=x and y=x² meet at x=0 and x=1; the area between them is 1/6.

chapters.example: Find the area between y = x and y = x² from x = 0 to x = 1; show the area is 1/6.
chapters.trap: Integrating upper minus lower without checking which curve is on top; after intersections the order may swap.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2.1 and 2.2: definite integrals and antiderivatives.
chapters.leave: Leave area by double integrals and change of order to Unit 5; leave volumes and surfaces to Chapter 2.7.

chapters.idea: Arc length is the limit of lengths of small straight chords, so it is an integral of √(1+(dy/dx)²) or √((dx/dt)²+(dy/dt)²).
chapters.depth: Cover the arc length formula for y=f(x): L=∫ₐᵇ √(1+(f′(x))²) dx, and for x=x(t), y=y(t): L=∫ √((dx/dt)²+(dy/dt)²) dt. Define L, a, b, t. Include simplifying the integrand before integrating and piecewise smooth curves. Some syllabi call this length of a curve. Keep to plane curves; curvature and torsion belong to Unit 6.

figure.aria: The curve y=(2/3)x^(3/2) from x=0 to 3; its arc length is 14/3.

chapters.example: Find the arc length of y = (2/3)x^(3/2) from x = 0 to x = 3; show that L = 14/3.
chapters.trap: Forgetting to square f′(x) or losing the square root; also forgetting that the formula needs a smooth curve or splitting at corners.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2.1 and 2.2; Unit 1 derivative rules and the chain rule.
chapters.leave: Leave space curves, curvature and torsion to Unit 6; leave surface area of revolution to Chapter 2.7.

chapters.idea: A solid of revolution is sliced into disks or washers, and its surface is made of thin bands, so both volume and area become integrals.
chapters.depth: Advanced: only a few universities teach this. Cover volume by disks V=π∫ₐᵇ (R(x))² dx and washers V=π∫ₐᵇ ((R(x))²−(r(x))²) dx for rotation about the x-axis; mention shells for rotation about the y-axis. Cover surface area S=2π∫ₐᵇ y√(1+(dy/dx)²) dx when y=f(x)≥0 rotates about the x-axis. Define R as outer radius, r as inner radius, and y as the curve height. Keep to single integrals.

figure.aria: The curve y=√x from x=0 to 4; rotating it about the x-axis gives volume 8π.

chapters.example: The curve y = √x from x = 0 to x = 4 is rotated about the x-axis. Find the volume; show that V = 8π.
chapters.trap: Squaring only R and not the whole radius, or using the surface formula without the square-root factor; also mixing disk and washer radii.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2.1, 2.2 and 2.5; algebra of circles and square roots.
chapters.leave: Leave surface integrals, Pappus theorems and multiple-integral volume to Unit 5 or Unit 6; leave numerical volumes to numerical methods.
